<SUMMARY>The period from May 29 to June 05, 2026, was characterized by escalating geopolitical tensions, significant advancements and challenges in the technology sector, and strategic realignments in critical resource supply chains. Geopolitically, China imposed a travel ban on New Zealand lawmakers following their visit to Taiwan, while the US-Iran conflict saw congressional action to limit US involvement and continued rhetoric regarding potential escalation. In the technology sphere, the AI boom drove substantial revenue growth in Taiwan's semiconductor industry and prompted major investments, yet also led to market volatility, as seen with Broadcom's revenue miss. Europe moved decisively towards tech sovereignty with new initiatives, and the US advanced defense integration with Israel. Critical minerals and energy security remained key concerns, with India announcing processing incentives and the EU investing in African resources amid ongoing supply chain disruptions from the Iran conflict.</SUMMARY>
<EWS>Reports from serious journalists and former CIA analysts indicate that Iran may be close to demonstrating a nuclear weapon, raising significant strategic questions. The ongoing US-Iran conflict has led to increased oil prices and market falls, impacting global energy supply chains and exposing Europe's energy vulnerabilities. Broadcom's second-quarter revenue miss and subsequent market value loss highlight precarious expectations and potential volatility within the AI semiconductor sector. The Commerce Department admitted failure to enforce AI export controls on China, contributing to disruptions in global semiconductor supply chains. Artificial intelligence companies are warning of potential bottlenecks in the AI supply chain.</EWS>
<EXEC>
**Asia:**
China imposed a travel ban on a group of New Zealand lawmakers who visited Taiwan in May. The Southern Taiwan Science Park (STSP) reported revenue of nearly NT$1.1 trillion (approx. US$35.04 billion) for January to April 2026, an increase of 21.3% compared to the same period in 2025, driven by the semiconductor industry. Applied Materials plans to expand its Southeast Asia workforce by approximately 25% this year, adding at least 1,000 workers primarily in Singapore, which is becoming a more significant manufacturing, logistics, and advanced-packaging hub. The ASEAN region faces serious sustainability challenges due to its data center boom, despite these centers being critical enablers of the digital economy.

**Europe:**
The European Parliament switched to the Qwant search engine from Google, signaling Europe's strategic move towards tech independence. The EU unveiled a tech sovereignty package aimed at boosting European tech firms and limiting access for dominant US rivals, acknowledging that the bloc trails behind the US and Asia in AI, chips, cloud services, and data centers. Nintendo confirmed plans to launch versions of its Switch 2 hardware in the EU that will allow users to easily replace the battery, complying with a new EU regulation set to go into effect in February 2027.

**Americas:**
Broadcom's second-quarter revenue of $22.19 billion missed estimates of $22.27 billion, leading to a loss of over $250 billion in market value for the company. Despite this, Broadcom's CEO expects AI-driven demand to provide visibility through 2028, highlighting AI's transformative impact on the semiconductor industry. Georgia Governor Brian Kemp defended data centers against proposals to pause new facility construction, calling such bids "irresponsible."

<LITHO>
**Asia:**
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) Chairman C.C. Wei stated that CoPoS (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate) technology could scale within years, driven by the AI surge. The Southern Taiwan Science Park (STSP) recorded revenue of nearly NT$1.1 trillion for January to April 2026, surpassing the NT$1 trillion mark on the strength of the semiconductor boom. AMD committed more than $10 billion to Taiwan's AI supply chain. China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) stated that US export controls are disrupting global semiconductor supply chains.

**Americas:**
TSMC is planning $165 billion US fabs and is expanding its land for AI chip production in the US. Infineon is set to exit its Mexico backend semiconductor operations and is reviewing a site sale. Global semiconductor equipment billings reached US$36.55 billion in the first quarter of 2026.

**Europe:**
The EU CHIPS Act 2.0 proposal has been released, confirming photonics as a new structural addition to EU policy, indicating a thematic bullish outlook for the European photonics sector. Europe's sweeping tech sovereignty plan aims to boost its chip industry.

<REE>
**Africa:**
The EU is investing billions in South Africa as China continues to tighten its grip on critical minerals. Brazil holds one of the largest lithium reserves globally, with exploration barely begun, contrasting with the global rush to mine lithium from Congo and Chile.

**Oceania:**
The US issued a "slavery finding" against Australia. This action occurred in the context of President Donald Trump's past use of tariffs to increase power over other countries.

<GEO>
**Asia:**
China imposed a travel ban on a group of New Zealand lawmakers after their visit to Taiwan in May. China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Xinhua News stated that US abuse of export controls is disrupting global semiconductor industrial and supply chains.

**Americas:**
The Trump administration decided to dismantle most of a $386 million federal ocean-observing network, which scientists use to understand climate change impacts on currents and marine ecosystems.

**Oceania:**
The US "slavery finding" against Australia, linked to the Trump administration's broader use of tariffs against countries, highlights ongoing trade and geopolitical tensions.

<MILITARY>
</MILITARY>
<CONCLUSION>The period underscores a deepening global contest across technological, economic, and geopolitical fronts. The AI boom continues to drive semiconductor industry growth, particularly in Asia, but also introduces market volatility and supply chain vulnerabilities. Europe is asserting its tech sovereignty to mitigate reliance on US and Asian tech giants. Geopolitical tensions are evident in China's response to Taiwan visits and the persistent US-Iran conflict, which significantly impacts global energy markets. Strategic competition over critical minerals is intensifying, with both the EU and India implementing policies to secure their supply chains. The US administration's actions, from trade findings against allies to domestic environmental policy shifts, contribute to a dynamic and sometimes unpredictable global landscape.</CONCLUSION>

<INDIA>India's Global Capability Centres (GCCs) are rapidly outpacing traditional IT services due to multinational corporations seeking more control over intellectual property, data, and AI, leveraging India's deep talent pool and offering higher compensation. India plans to unveil incentives totaling around ₹3,000 crores for lithium and nickel processing to bolster its electric vehicle supply chain. Experts highlighted Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) as a solution for reliable, clean, and uninterrupted electricity to address critical power supply constraints in India's defense production and data center sectors.</INDIA>

<WEST_ASIA>Rumors from serious journalists, including Pepe Escobar and former CIA analyst Larry Johnson, suggest that Iran is preparing to demonstrate a nuclear weapon, with Larry Johnson further speculating Iran may have already built one. The US House of Representatives passed a resolution directing President Donald Trump to withdraw American forces from hostilities with Iran unless authorized by Congress. President Trump stated that a US ground operation against Iran is not necessary, citing the effectiveness of ongoing bombing campaigns. US-Israel defense integration is advancing at an unprecedented level through a provision in the House version of the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu told CNBC that Israel and the US are prepared to attack Iran again if necessary, leading to increased oil prices and market drops. US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth stated at the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore that the United States will no longer "subsidize" the defense of "wealthy" allies. Kuwait Petroleum Company estimates 10-12 weeks to restore oil output after the Strait of Hormuz reopens. The Middle East conflict is significantly impacting Asia-Pacific power markets and disrupting global oil and gas supply. US-Iran peace talks have stalled, and the Iran war has exposed Europe’s energy vulnerabilities.</WEST_ASIA>

<FINAL_CONCLUSION>The coming weeks will likely see sustained volatility in global markets, driven by continued uncertainty in the AI semiconductor sector and the escalating geopolitical landscape in West Asia. US export control enforcement and China's responses will remain key determinants of global supply chain stability. Further developments in Iran's nuclear program could trigger significant international repercussions. Nations will continue to prioritize critical mineral security and tech sovereignty, potentially leading to additional investments and trade policy shifts.</FINAL_CONCLUSION>
